topic_info.title: Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease (CPPD) or Pseudogout

list.listitem: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease previously known as pseudogout is arthritis caused by the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals in articular tissue. C

Patients typically present with a fairly rapid unilateral pain in the knee, wrist, shoulder, ankle, or elbow; and should be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients with gout. Use the 2023 ACR/EULAR diagnostic criteria () to help make the diagnosis.C
In acute mono-arthritis, septic arthritis should also be ruled out. C
In patients younger than 60 years of age, underlying metabolic conditions associated with CPPD diseases such as hyperparathyroidism or hemochromatosis, should be investigated. C

There is no definitive treatment for CPPD disease, but analgesics including NSAIDs, intraarticular colchicine or systemic glucocorticoids, and the interleukin 1 beta-antagonist anakinra, may have a role in the treatment of CPPD disease. C

background.definition: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition (CPPD) disease previously known as pseudogout is an acute inflammatory arthritis resulting from the deposition of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals within articular tissue, most frequently fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage.

list.listitem: Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate deposition disease (CPPD) is a disease of older adults.
CPPD disease affects 4% to 7% of the population.
There is an equal occurrence between both males and females.
Radiographic CPPD disease is present in up to 44% of patients > 84 years of age with the prevalence doubling each decade over the age of 60 years old.
Older age. More than 80% of patients are over 60 years of age.
Most cases of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition (CPPD) disease are idiopathic.

Risk factors for developing crystal deposition include joint trauma, early adult life knee malalignment, osteoarthritis, gout, lower bone mineral density, and a variety of metabolic and endocrine disorders (e.g., hyperparathyroidism, hemochromatosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypophosphatasia).
Medications possibly associated with an increased risk of CPPD disease include intraarticular hyaluronan, loop diuretics, granulocyte–macrophage colony-stimulating factor, and pamidronate.
Other medications associated with CPPD disease in case reports include pegfilgrastim and bisphosphonates.

Familial CPPD disease should be considered in persons less than age 60 years old and in those with a positive family history. Two genetic mutations associated with familial CPPD disease involve the CCAL2 locus on chromosome 5p and the CCAL1 locus on chromosome 8.

CPPD occurs in the articular cartilage pericellular matrix. Chondrocytes express nucleoside triphosphate pyrophosphohydrolase (NTPPH) enzymes on their cell membrane. These enzymes play a normal role in bone calcification. The overactivity of these enzymes catalyze the production of pyrophosphate which binds with calcium phosphate to form calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) in the immediate environment of the chondrocytes.
Enhanced activity of the defective ANK gene increases extracellular but decreases intracellular pyrophosphate, promoting crystal apatite deposition in the joint.

Aging cartilage predisposes to CPPD deposition and CPPD deposition itself increases the production of inorganic pyrophosphate, decreases levels of pyrophosphatases, and reduces cartilage glycosaminoglycans that inhibit crystal formation.
CPPD crystals in the joint are phagocytized by neutrophils which release a glycopeptide chemotactic for other neutrophils which in turn triggers the inflammatory cascade.

Mitogenic response of fibroblasts to stimulation with CPPD crystals is accompanied by induction and secretion of collagenase and neutral proteases, implying a role for the crystals in the pathogenesis of both synovial proliferation and joint damage in chronic basic calcium phosphate crystal-associated arthropathy.
The molecular mechanism of CPPD disease also demonstrates overproduction of interleukin-1.

Diseases that create metabolic products (such as calcium in hyperparathyroidism, iron in hemochromatosis, or copper in Wilson's disease) predispose to chondrocalcinosis either from direct effects on cartilage or inhibition of inorganic pyrophosphatases; these conditions must be looked for in patients younger than 60 years.
Patients typically present with fairly rapid unilateral pain in the knee, wrist, shoulder, ankle, or elbow; consider it in the differential diagnosis of patients with gout and septic arthritis. C
Definitive diagnosis requires the presence of either crowned dens syndrome or synovial fluid analysis demonstrating CPP crystals in a joint with swelling, tenderness, or pain. C
Use the 2023 ACR/EULA diagnostic criteria (). C
Radiographs and ultrasound may reveal punctate and linear radiodense and hyperechoic areas respectively in fibrocartilage and hyaline cartilage. C

Differential.Differential_Features: On polarized microscopy, negatively birefringent crystals visualized; mostly affects the first MTP joint or knee
Bilateral symmetrical small joint pain and stiffness
Synovial fluid analysis shows WBC counts of >50,000 per mm3 or a PMN percentage of > 75 %
Rarely involves metacarpophalangeal, wrist, elbow, shoulder, or ankle, negative for crystals
Incidental finding of chondrocalcinosis on radiographs
Loss of joint sensory modalities such as pain, temperature, and joint position
Calcifying or ossifying mass lesions within the spine

list.listitem: In 2023, the European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) and the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) formulated a new validated diagnostic criteria for the diagnosis of CPPD. It is summarized in . .

The CPPD disease classification criteria should be applied in the following order: 1. Entry criterion: Ever had at least one episode of joint pain, swelling, or tenderness. 2. Absolute exclusion criteria: All symptoms are more likely explained by an alternative condition (such as rheumatoid arthritis, gout, psoriatic arthritis, OA, etc.). 3. Sufficient criteria: Presence of either crowned dens syndrome or synovial fluid analysis demonstrating CPP crystals in a joint with swelling, tenderness, or pain. An individual is classified as having CPPD disease if the entry criterion is met, exclusion criteria are not met, and at least one sufficient criterion is fulfilled.
If none of the sufficient criteria are present, an individual is classified as having CPPD disease if the sum of the points per the scoring criteria is >56 points..See scoring criteria in .

Scoring of criteria Items can be scored if they were ever present during a patient's lifetime. If a patient fulfills >1 item in a given domain, only the highest weighted item will be scored. Imaging of at least one symptomatic joint by CR, US, CT, or DECT is required.
Patients typically present with unilateral pain in the knee, wrist, shoulder, ankle, or elbow. Onset is often rapid.
The presentation may include self-limited, acute, sub-acute, chronic or acute-on-chronic attacks of arthritis involving one or several extremity joints.

Approximately 89% of patients with CPPD are monoarticular or oligoarticular while the remaining 11% are polyarticular. European League Against Rheumatism (EULAR) task force classification of CPPD disease include the following: 1) Asymptomatic CPPD disease: No clinical symptoms and may be isolated chondrocalcinosis (CC) or OA with CC. Usually incidental. 2) Osteoarthritis with CPPD: OA and CPPD on a joint that may be identified on imaging or histologic examination. 3) Acute CPP crystal arthritis (replaces the term pseudogout): Acute and self-limiting CPPD. 4) Chronic CPP crystal inflammatory arthritis: Chronic inflammatory arthritis associated with CPPD
Attacks closely resemble urate gout with accompanying signs of severe inflammation.
Trauma, severe medical illness, intraarticular procedures, and parathyroidectomy frequently provoke attacks or flares of CPPD disease.
The knee is involved in over 50% of all acute attacks.

Synovial Fluid Analysis (SFA): The current gold standard in diagnosing CPPD is SFA with polarized light microscopy (PLM). Positively birefringent CPPD crystals are visualized by compensated polarized light microscopy. Phagocytized crystals within polymorphonuclear leucocytes may also be present. However, small crystal sizes, the presence of other crystal types, glass artefacts and cellular uptake of monosodium urate (MSU) can pose uncertainties in the clinical analysis of synovial fluids. Raman Spectroscopy integrated with polarized light microscopy addresses these diagnostic challenges.

Radiographs: have a sensitivity of 40% with high specificity for chondrocalcinosis.They may reveal punctate and linear radiodense areas in fibrocartilage, hyaline cartilage, ligaments, and joint capsule. Chondrocalcinosis is detected in approximately 29% to 93% of patients with CPPD disease. Calcification of the gastrocnemius tendon and chondrocalcinosis on radiographs also support the diagnosis of CPPD disease.While chondrocalcinosis may occur in up to 40% of patients with clinically significant disease, it is not exclusively present in patients with CPPD disease.

Ultrasonography (US): May reveal hyperechoic bands or spots or deposits in the articular cartilage, fibrocartilage, and bursae., One study reported a sensitivity of 69% and specificity of 97% for intracartilaginous hyperechoic spots for the diagnosis of CPPD, so their presence is strong evidence in favor of CPPD. High-resolution ultrasound is even more sensitive.

listitem.strong: A targeted US scanning protocol of two joints bilaterally plus the target ( inflamed) joint showed an accuracy of > 90 % for the diagnosis of crystal arthritis.

list.listitem: Another study showed bilateral US assessment of knees, wrists and hips had a sensitivity of 97% and a specificity of 100% for the diagnosis of CPPD disease (LR+ 97, LR- 0.03).
Traditional X-ray has a sensitivity of 39% for detecting chondrocalcinosis. Ultrasound has a specificity of 96% and sensitivity of 87% (LR+ 7.4, LR- 0.05).

CT scan: CT is useful in the evaluation of the spine and also in Crowned Dens Syndrome. High-resolution CT or DECT (Dual energy CT for detecting crystals in tissues) have good sensitivity and specificity
MRI without contrast: Not that sensitive but may be useful in patients with neurological symptoms
See algorithm in . Consider the diagnosis if history and physical examination findings are suggestive. Obtain labs to look for precipitating factors/conditions, especially if younger than 60 years.
X-ray the involved joint, and obtain fluid, if the effusion is present.
Treat based on the identified cause.
Acute attack: rest and immobilization, NSAIDs, intraarticular or oral steroids, oral colchicine. C
Recurrent attacks (>3 attacks/year): oral colchicine and/ or NSAID therapy. The interleukin 1 beta-antagonist anakinra, may have a role in the treatment of persistent CPPD disease. C
Treatment recommendations are generally based on case reports, case series, and expert opinion. Randomized trials are lacking. C
No treatment is recommended for patients with asymptomatic CPPD disease. C

There is currently no treatment to remove CPP crystals from the joints. Treatment is primarily symptomatic since there is no known drug that prevents the progression of CPPD arthritis-induced joint destruction.

NSAIDs or colchicine may be used during acute inflammation. A short course of oral or systemic steroids is useful in the presence of contraindications to NSAIDs or colchicine. Corticotrophin (ACTH) may also be effective for acute attacks.

Use of the interleukin 1 beta-antagonist anakinra at 100 mg SC daily has been reported to be helpful to control flares in patients with CPP crystal-induced arthritis for which conventional therapies are ineffective or contraindicated, based entirely on case reports and case series though.
Other options for resistant acute CPPD arthritis include anti-TNF therapy such as adalimumab and IL-6 inhibiting monoclonal antibody such as tocilizumab.
In a small uncontrolled series, methotrexate (7.5 mg weekly) appeared to be effective; it can be considered when other treatments fail.

Initial treatment includes NSAIDS like naproxen; if there is no response to it colchicine may be used. Prednisone, methotrexate, or hydroxychloroquine may be used for resistant cases. None of these treatments are backed by randomized trial evidence.
Consider prophylaxis for patients with recurrent attacks of CPPD disease (>3 attacks a year).
Prophylaxis for patients with acute attacks of CPPD disease may be achieved with the use of colchicine or oral NSAID (with gastroprotective treatment if indicated).
Colchicine (0.6 mg twice daily, maximum 1.8 mg/day) has been recommended for recurring CPPD disease.
Surgery (eg, joint replacement) can restore function and relieve pain in progressive destructive large joint arthropathy.
Intraarticular steroid injections are indicated in monoarticluar presentation. It is preferable to use NSAIDs, colchicine and systemic steroids if two or more joints are involved.
Joint immobilization and ice or cool pack application are recommended. Removal of crystals through joint aspiration is sometimes performed.
Patients should be provided education and advice as well as strengthening exercises and aerobic fitness training (if physically possible).
If the patient is overweight, weight loss is helpful.
Most patients with acute CPPD disease can expect significant improvement in their symptoms over days to weeks.
Acute CPPD is associated with increased risk for fractures, nephrolithiasis, acute coronary syndrome, and stroke
Patients with chronic CPPD disease often have chronic joint pain and loss of function despite treatment. C
Chronic CPPD disease may increase risk of both hip and knee arthroplasties.

algorithm.title: Approach to the Patient with Suspected CPPD disease/Pseudogout.

cell.label: History (fever, associated condition) and/or Physical exam finding (painful, swollen joint)

Labs: CBC, ESR, Uric acid, serum calcium, phosphate, magnesium, alkaline phosphatase, ferritin level, transferrin saturation. (Treat any underlying chemical abnormality.) Radiology: X-ray affected joint. Joint effusion
(a) SF WBC >2,000/mm3: Inflammatory arthritis likely. (b) SF WBC >50,000/mm3: Suspect septic arthritis. (c) SF WBC >100,000/mm3: Septic arthritis until proven otherwise.
Pseudogout/CPPD disease: CPPD. Positively birefringent. Rhomboid crystals.
Gout: Monosodium urate. Negatively birefringent. Needle-shaped crystals.

footnotes.footnote: Abbreviations: CBC, complete blood count; ESR, erythrocyte sedimentation rate; WBC, white blood count; CPPD, calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate; SF, synovial fluid.

Synovial fluid crystal analysis from a symptomatic joint

None of the following findings or no imaging performed

Number of peripheral joints with evidence of CPPD on any imaging modality, regardless of symptoms
